extracted.subtask_description: Practical handbook guidance for beat reporting, interviewing, gathering facts, and organizing news copy for daily newspapers; covers routine tactics, professional ethics, and story-structure principles. Aimed at reporters learning how to get and write news quickly and honorably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for the beat
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter is held responsible for all the news occurring on his run; failure or being scooped by a rival is severely judged by the city editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be diligent about every news source on your run; a scoop even of a few minutes is the 'unpardonable sin' with the city editor. Never neglect any source on your beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark Runs
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain places (garages, delicatessen stores, florists, caterers, etc.) are 'dark runs'—consistently productive of news but must be kept 'dark' (sensitive/confidential).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate friendships with proprietors who often know patrons' orders or mishaps. These sources can yield exclusive facts about prominent people. Use skill and discretion to encourage them; include several such sources in daily rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of wide acquaintance
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately cultivate friendships and acquaintances everywhere—in stores, on streetcars, at clubs—because many important news items come from casual contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather items from merchants, cabmen, preachers, barkeepers, patrolmen, porters, etc. Guard confidences zealously and distinguish between publishable information from strangers and confidential information from friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish publishable information vs. confidences
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter must not suppress news obtained while on duty; publication or non-publication of confidential information is the city editor's decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information given by strangers while on duty should be published. Information given confidentially by a friend (at club or home) may not be used without that person's express permission; maintain personal and professional integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry essential tools when starting for a story
rubrics_metrics.description: When sent for a story, a reporter should have cards, plenty of paper and pencils, and a neat engraved business card.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep several sharp, soft-lead pencils and folded copy paper for note-taking. Display professional insignia as little as possible; a business card is often the only means of admittance to a house.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the telephone for reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The telephone is useful for running down rumors, obtaining unimportant interviews, and getting stories the persons want published—but is not generally advisable for important stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on telephone for crucial verification because you miss facial expressions and gestures; use phone to verify rumors (e.g., call a bakery) but go in person to the scene when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use city maps to locate incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult a city map when you do not know precise locations to learn where to go.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A beginner should use maps to find corners; experienced reporters ought to know the city so well they need no map, but a map is valuable while learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding the place—start with the policeman
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon arrival, go first to the patrolman on the beat, who usually knows main details and can point out the house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the policeman knows nothing, systematically inquire at houses, neighborhood stores (groceries, bakeries, saloons, barber shops) and keep persisting until you locate the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular reports to the city editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Report progress regularly to the city editor when on assignment—sometimes hourly—especially for afternoon papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent reporting keeps the city editor informed; fresh small details may interest readers during multiple editions. Some editors require hourly calls even with no news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retracing one's work and determination
rubrics_metrics.description: If initial inquiries fail, a reporter must retrace work, re-inquire patrolmen, revisit houses and shops, and exhaust every available clue before giving up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check hospitals, corner houses in adjoining blocks, children playing nearby, and other unconventional leads. Never give up until every measure suited to the circumstances has been tried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaining access for an interview
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a business card, polite inquiry, and tact to gain access to injured or reluctant subjects; express interest naturally if admission is refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is in a hotel, club, or house, send or present a card as appropriate. If told the person cannot be seen, express concern and ask questions that lead toward an interview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six requirements for successful interviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly there are six requirements: a pleasing presence; the ability to question judiciously; quick perception of news in chance remarks; a retentive memory; the power to detect falsehood readily; and the ability to single out characteristic phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat interviewing as consultation for publication; prepare to meet these technical and personal requirements to extract useful and publishable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasing presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain immaculate person and linen, tact, courtesy, and qualities that make the interviewee comfortable; avoid obvious flattery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unshaven face or shabby collar harms a reporter's reception. Tact is as important as dress; flattery is quickly detected and resented by intelligent interviewees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtesy in interviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Always be a gentleman; never allow anger, because it causes loss of control and creates lifelong hostility from the interviewee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kindness begets kindness; anger ruins memory and questioning ability and will make the subject an enemy of the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asking questions—judicious questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with topics that let the person talk about themselves or their work; keep silent often; guide the conversation back if it runs afield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the subject run; interrupting for the reporter's views is a cub's mistake. Accept some irrelevant talk to bring the subject back gracefully to the point of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and avoid persons seeking advertisement
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people talk for the sake of seeing their names in print; these 'advertisement' interviewees should be avoided by reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize those who supply material merely for publicity; advertisements are the domain of the advertising manager and should not be treated as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling persons refusing to talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Men who refuse to talk are often well acquainted with the world; the reporter must be careful, keep temper sweet, and if threatened with legal action, report facts to the city editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be daunted by threats to sue; get facts and present them with the subject's hinted threat to the city editor for a publication decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliciting secrets—leading and circling back
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert reluctant informants into unwitting divulgers by leading away from the topic and circling back when they are off guard; the art is to observe without betraying that you noticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Star reporters receive indiscreet utterances as though bored so the subject does not realize the blunder until reading it the next day. Quick perception of news in chance remarks is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retentive memory
rubrics_metrics.description: A good memory is necessary because many interviewees are frightened by notebooks; record facts promptly after the interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlate and hold facts in mind until you can write them down. Some use small cards, pencil stubs, or even occasional notes on cuffs to avoid alarming the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of shorthand—sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Shorthand is useful for accuracy but should not be overused because it can deaden the presentation and make the story lifeless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shorthand for occasional exact statements, but avoid making it the reporter's crutch; being too intent on exact words can cause missing the spirit of the interview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise questions in interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing a sheet of typewritten questions forces definite answers and ensures the reporter knows the exact purpose of the visit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Busy public figures resent visitors who do not know what they want; precise questions and brevity lead to better receptions and more productive interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn the subject's career in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a good general knowledge of the subject's career and accomplishments so you won't force them into excessive detail or technical explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult morgue files, encyclopedias, Who's Who, local knowledgeable people, and staff before interviewing prominent figures to appear informed and expedite the visit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to detect falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider an informant's mental caliber and motives; many witnesses are biased or excited and do not give accurate accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate possible motives—for self-exploitation, grudges, or prejudice—and discount or corroborate statements accordingly to avoid libel or inaccuracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question everyone connected to the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview all persons connected with an event—witnesses, servants, janitors, maids, chauffeurs, and even children—as they may provide facts others conceal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children often give less colored and more connected accounts. Humble persons may divulge facts that servants or detectives would conceal for money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate a person's previous record
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquire into past history (divorce, criminal record, previous public notice) as such facts aid identification and provide material for conjecture and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlation of present and past facts may become the main story. Make every effort to obtain background information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record full details
rubrics_metrics.description: Record all details—names, addresses, telephone numbers, and photographs—because it is easier to discard unneeded material than to return for neglected information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect telephone numbers and picture copies; many papers promise to return photographs. Even incidental persons at first may become important later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting names and addresses correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Get initials, street addresses, and spellings correctly to avoid libel suits and offended subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistakes in initials or addresses have started libel suits; double-check spellings and addresses carefully before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling speeches—advance copies and releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain advance copies ('release' stories) and photographs of speeches to quote correctly; respect release dates for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers scrupulously observe release dates; editors will punish violations (e.g., loss of telegraphic wires). With advance copies, you may write at leisure or even skip attending if permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attending lectures—reporting technique
rubrics_metrics.description: If no advance copy is available, attend the lecture, obtain tickets in advance, sit near a table, and report by topics with occasional verbatim passages of pithy remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't try to take lectures word-for-word; capture the significance and spirit. If a verbatim report is required, a stenographer should be sent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter’s honor—obtain stories honestly
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain stories with determination but honor; do not use illegal or dishonest methods (breaking and entering, eavesdropping, bribery, fake stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputable newspapers want gentlemen, not lawbreakers; faking or willful distortion will result in dismissal and is ethically condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize material before writing
rubrics_metrics.description: On the way back to the office, arrange facts so you can write quickly, accurately, and interestingly—the organization of material speeds composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a definite plan or mental outline for the story so you spend less time rearranging jumbled notes and more time composing effective sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed as a primary asset
rubrics_metrics.description: Next to accuracy, speed is a newspaper man's most valuable asset; many value speed even above trustworthiness of statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop methods to reorganize notes mentally or on paper while returning, and have a definite plan for the story to get copy into the city room quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy through reorganization
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully reorder and understand your notes before writing to avoid including irrelevant facts or omitting illegible but important items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited mental power requires allocating attention to recognizing facts, typing keys, and composing; messy notes reduce the energy left for clear expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest/Angle selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Every story must possess a specific point or 'angle' (the heinousness of the crime, the loneliness of the widow, etc.) which is largely determined by selection of details and paper policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and arrange details with the paper's policy and readers' interests in mind; the same incident can be presented humorously, pathetically, or otherwise by choosing different details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four orders of organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Material may be organized in four orders: time order, space order, climactic order, and complex order; most news stories use time order or combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximately 95% of news uses time order; choose the organizational order (or combination) that best supports the story's angle and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time order (chronological organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time order arranges incidents chronologically and is the simplest and most commonly used structure for news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chronological arrangement to narrate incidents clearly; the text gives an example headline and follow-up chronology.
